rationale: This mixed-methods empirical study investigates drinking water service disparities across 34 informal settlements (slums) in Hyderabad, India, using household surveys, stakeholder interviews, and water quality assessments (satisfying Criteria 1, 3, and 4). While the abstract frames its analysis around governance, decision-making frameworks, and institutional and economic dimensions via the S.I.T.E. valuation framework, full-text inspection is required to determine whether it analyses specific legal, administrative, tenure/slum-notification, tariff, or utility-discretion rules governing service access under the narrow Criterion 2 reading. In accordance with Phase 5 rules against prematurely excluding ambiguous informal-settlement governance studies, the narrow decision is 'unsure'.
plain_vs_narrow_note: Under the literal/plain Criterion 2 wording, the study clearly qualifies for inclusion because it empirically examines institutional and governance dimensions of drinking water access across 34 slum areas in Hyderabad. Under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, the abstract leaves unclear whether the institutional and economic dimensions analysed include concrete legal/administrative rules (such as slum notification/tenure eligibility, utility allocation rules, tariffs/subsidies, or administrative discretion) versus a purely conceptual planning/participatory valuation framework (S.I.T.E.), warranting full-text retrieval ('unsure').

evidence_quotes.quote: This study investigates the governance dimensions of water service provision in Hyderabad, India, focusing on disparities in access among slum communities.

Through a mixed-methods approach involving household surveys, stakeholder interviews, and water quality assessments across 34 slum areas, the research identifies critical gaps in existing decision-making frameworks.
Findings reveal that while technical aspects are routinely considered, socio-health, institutional, and economic dimensions are often neglected, leading to uneven service delivery.
